'''''Quercus infectoria''''' or the '''Aleppo oak''' is a species of [[oak]] well known for producing [[gall]]s (called '''manjakani''' in Malaysia, '''majuphal''' in India) that have been traditionally used for centuries in Asia medicinally while also used in [[Tanning (leather)|softening leather]] and in making black dye and ink.<ref name=":0" />

==Description==
''Quercus infectoria'' is a small tree, growing to {{convert|4|to|6|ft|abbr=off|m|0|order=flip}} in height.{{Citation needed|date= March 2022}} The stems are crooked, shrubby looking with smooth and bright-green [[leaves]] borne on short petioles of {{convert|3-4|cm|abbr=off|frac=4}} long. The leaves are bluntly mucronate, rounded, smooth, unequal at the base and shiny on the upper side.

The galls arise on young branches of the tree when [[gall wasp]]s<ref name="TradMed">{{cite book |author1 = Muhamad Z|author2 = Mustafa AM|title = Traditional Malay Medicinal Plants.|year = 1994|location = Kuala Lumpur|publisher = Penerbit Fajar Bakti Sdn Bhd}}</ref> sting the oak tree and deposit their larvae. The chemical reaction causes an abnormality in the tree, causing hard balls to be formed. They are [[wikt:corrugated|corrugated]] in appearance.

=== Gall chemistry ===
The galls from ''Quercus infectoria'' contain the highest naturally occurring level of [[tannin]], approximately 50–70%,<ref name="SyringicAcid">{{cite journal |author1=Dar MS |author2=Ikram M |title=Studies on Quercus infectoria; isolation of syringic acid and determination of its central depressive activity. |journal=Planta Medica |year=1979 |volume=35 |issue=2 |pages=156–161 |publisher=Planta Med.|doi=10.1055/s-0028-1097197 |pmid=419182 |bibcode=1979PlMed..35..156D }}</ref> as well as [[syringic acid]], [[β-sitosterol]], [[amentoflavone]], hexamethyl ether, isocryptomerin, methyl betulate, methyl oleanate, and hexagalloyl glucose.<ref name="SyringicAcid" /><ref name=":1" /> They also contain 2–4% each of [[Gallic acid|gallic]] and [[ellagic acid]] that are polymerized to make tannins.<ref name="Ikram">{{cite journal |author1=Ikram M |author2=Nowshad F |title=Constituents of Quercus infectoria. |journal=Planta Medica |year=1997 |volume=31 |issue=3 |pages=286–7 |publisher=Planta Med|doi=10.1055/s-0028-1097531 |pmid=866492 }}[https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/866492?dopt=Abstract PubMed]</ref><ref name=":2">{{cite book |author1=Evans WC |title=Pharmacopoeial and related drugs of biological origin. |year=1996 |publisher=WB Saunders Co. Ltd. |location=London }}</ref><ref name=":3">{{cite book |author1=Wiart C |author2=Kumar A |title= Practical Handbook of Pharmacognosy. |year=2001 |publisher=Pearson Education Malaysia Sdn Bhd |location=Malaysia }}</ref> Tannins have been used for hundreds of years for medical purposes and are currently indispensable in dermatology<ref>{{cite journal | author1=Regina Fölster-Holst M.D. | author2=Eva Latussek Ph.D. | title=Synthetic Tannins in Dermatology — A Therapeutic Option in a Variety of Pediatric Dermatoses | journal=Pediatric Dermatology | year=2007 | volume=24 | issue=3 | pages=296–301 | publisher=Department of Dermatology, Venerology and Allergology, University of Schleswig-Holstein, Kiel |doi=10.1111/j.1525-1470.2007.00406.x | pmid=17542884 | s2cid=25310247 }}</ref> and have been used for tanning of leather.

==== Tannins ====
Tannins comprise a large group of natural products widely distributed in the plant kingdom. They have a great structural diversity, but are usually divided into two basic groups: the hydrolyzable type and the condensed type. Hydrolyzable tannins include the commonly occurring gallic and ellagic acid contained in the nut galls.

Hydrolyzable tannins are present in many different plant species but are found in particularly high concentrations in nut galls growing on ''[[Rhus semialata]]'' (Chinese and Korean gallotannins) and ''Quercus infectoria'' (Turkish and Chinese gallotannins), the seedpods of ''[[Caesalpinia spinosa]]'' (Tara tannins), and the fruits of ''[[Terminalia chebula]]''. The gallic and ellagic acid hydrolyzable tannins react with proteins to produce typical tanning effects; medicinally, this is important to topically treat inflamed or ulcerated tissues. They also contribute to most of the astringent property of ''manjakani'' and in small insignificant doses, can be used for skin whitening and killing microorganisms.

Although both types of tannin have been used to treat diseases in traditional medicine, the [[Hydrolysis|hydrolyzable]] tannins have long been considered official medicinal agents in Europe and North America. They have been included in many [[pharmacopoeia]]s, in the older editions in particular, and are specifically referred to as tannic acid. These were recommended for treatment of inflammation and [[ulcer]]ation, including topical application for skin diseases and internal use for intestinal ulceration and diarrhea. In China, tannin-containing substances, such as galls, [[pomegranate]] rinds, and [[Terminalia (plant)|terminalia]] fruits, are used in several medicinal preparations.

==Distribution==
''Quercus infectoria'' is indigenous to parts of [[southern Europe]] ([[Greece]] and the East [[Aegean Sea|Aegean]] Islands) and the [[Middle East]] ([[Turkey]], [[Cyprus]], [[Iran]], [[Iraq]], [[Lebanon]], [[Syria]], [[Israel]], [[Palestine]], and [[Jordan]]).<ref>{{cite book | chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-94-007-4053-2_3 | doi=10.1007/978-94-007-4053-2_3 | chapter=Quercus infectoria | title=Edible Medicinal and Non-Medicinal Plants | date=2012 | last1=Lim | first1=T. K. | pages=16–26 | isbn=978-94-007-4052-5 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Azab |first=Abdullatif |date=July 2025 |title=QUERCUS (OAK) TREES OF ISRAEL AND PALESTINE |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/393771218_QUERCUS_OAK_TREES_OF_ISRAEL_AND_PALESTINE |journal=World Journal of Pharmaceutical Research |volume=14 |issue=14 |pages=136–178 |via=ResearchGate}}</ref>

==Uses==
''Quercus infectoria'' can be used as a [[thickener]] in stews or mixed with cereals for making bread.<ref>{{cite book |author1=Stashia Eleaness |title=The extraction of essential oil from Quercus infectoria (Manjakani) galls using supercritical carbon dioxide pressure swing technique |author2=Rosland Abel |publisher=Faculty of Chemical Engineering |year=2013 |editor=Universiti Teknologi Malaysia |chapter=1}}</ref>

The "Aleppo tannin" is [[tannic acid]] gained from Aleppo oak galls, which display unique chemical properties essential in the preparation of gold [[Sol (colloid)|sols]] (colloids) used as markers in [[immunocytochemistry]].<ref>{{cite book |author=Frank Mayer |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MzT9eWxtmRgC&pg=PA216 |title=Electron Microscopy in Microbiology |publisher=Academic Press |year=1988 |isbn=9780080860497 |volume=20 |location=London |page=216 |access-date=17 May 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author=Gareth Griffiths |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZPDxCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA285 |title=Fine Structure Immunocytochemistry |publisher=Springer |year=1993 |isbn=978-3-642-77097-5 |location=Berlin & Heidelberg |page=185}}</ref>

Gall nut extracts are widely used in pharmaceuticals, medical laboratory techniques as well as inks which use "[[Aleppo tannin]]",<ref>[http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/13863/Aleppo-oak Encyclopædia Britannica, Aleppo oak ] |accessdate=17 May 2015</ref> food and feed additives, dyes, metallurgy, and [[leather tanning]].{{Citation needed|date=April 2026}}

The galls, locally known as ''manjakani'' in Malaysia, are used in combination with other herbs as drinking remedies by women after childbirth to restore the elasticity of the uterine wall, and in many vaginal tightening products.<ref name="TradMed" /> The extract of ''manjakani'' was claimed by the [[Ethnic Malays|Malay]] [[Kelantan]]ese to be highly beneficial for postpartum women. Hazardous effects of the extract were not reported so far. In addition, the Arabs, Persians, Indians, Malays and Chinese have traditionally used the galls after childbirth to treat vaginal discharge and related [[postpartum infections]].{{Citation needed|date=April 2026}}

Also known as ''majuphal'' in Indian traditional medicine, ''manjakani'' has been used as dental powder and in the treatment of toothache and gingivitis.<ref name=":0">{{cite book |author1=Kottakkal AVS. |title=Indian Medicinal Plants. |year=1995 |publisher=Orient Longman Ltd. |volume=4 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author1=Bhattacharjee SK. |title=Handbook of Medicinal Plants. |year=2001 |location=India |publisher=Pointer Publishers }}</ref>
